newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's ANZ posts profit rise, promises more.
newsitem.headline: Australia's ANZ posts profit rise, promises more.

text.p: Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd (ANZ) reported a six-percent rise in net profit for the 1995/96 year on Wednesday and predicted more profit growth in the current year despite tighter interest margins.
The A$1.12-billion (US$888-million) net profit for the year to September 30 was above analysts' expectations of about A$1.05 billion.
But the rise in earnings was due largely to strong performance from ANZ's overseas units and disguised a sharp rise in operating costs and a lower profit from ANZ's Australian operations.
After the release of the results, ANZ Chief Executive Don Mercer forecast these costs would fall and that profits would continue to rise in the current 1996/97 year.
Asked by reporters if he expected growth in ANZ's bottom line in 1996/97, Mercer said: "That's certainly what a lot of people are expecting. We expect it of ourselves."
His call came despite an earlier statement by the bank that interest margins in Australia and New Zealand were expected to continue to contract in the current year.
Mercer also predicted costs would decline in the later part of fiscal 1996/97.
"Our costs are going to be flat in the first half of next year and they will be coming down in the second half," he said.
However, banking analysts were not as ebullient about the earnings prospects for ANZ.

"On the cost side, (reductions) are possible. The question is how the revenue side will hold up and maybe the extent of pressure there will be a bit greater than (ANZ) is expecting," one Sydney-based analyst told Reuters.
Mercer said higher personnel costs were the main contributor to the rise in operating expenses to A$3.64 billion in 1995/96 from A$3.33 billion the previous year.
"It wasn't my bonus. I wish it had been," Mercer quipped.
Personnel expenses rose to A$1.86 billion for the year from A$1.62 billion, while other expenses such as rent and computer costs were either flat or slightly lower.
The bank said it planned to grow by expanding its successful international operations and to expand its credit card, funds management and investment banking services.

ANZ saw India as the most exciting offshore growth region, with the bank's 150-year-old presence under the Grindlays Bank brand leaving it well-positioned to take advantage of the country's developing economy, Mercer said.

"India is an economy which is opening to the world. We've got excellent connections and as India opens and its economic activity lifts, and in particular the cross-border activity lifts,...we're right in the thick of that," he said.
Mercer said ANZ was investing in new technology to link its 56 Indian branches in order to widen its retail banking operations there.
The chief executive said he was excited by the amount of investment European and U.S.-based customers were interested in directing toward India as well as other emerging markets.
